newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election still open, right looks to Chirac.
newsitem.headline: French election still open, right looks to Chirac.

text.p: Two weeks before the first round of voting, France's parliamentary election is still wide open despite a first opinion poll to show the ruling centre-right coalition rebuilding its lead, political analysts say.

The outcome of the vote, on which may hinge the stability of Europe's drive for a single currency, could depend on the skill with which conservative President Jacques Chirac plays his remaining cards.

Amid widespread indifference, accentuated by a spate of public holidays and non-political media events such as the Cannes Film Festival, the campaign for the snap May 25-June 1 vote has not yet settled on a decisive issue or argument.

Given the persistent unpopularity of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, a favourite target for the left and for snipers in his own camp, conservative politicians are looking to Chirac to rescue the campaign by intervening for a second time.
"Chirac hit the spot by pointing to the woeful record of the left. He should do it again because the race isn't won yet," centre-right Urban Affairs Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin said.

Until the weekend, a series of polls had shown the left-wing opposition gaining momentum. The Socialists, Communists and far-left, despite divisions over economic policy and a single European currency, had drawn level or overtaken the centre-right in voting intentions and were whittling away the conservative lead in seats, fanning anxiety in Chirac's camp.

Government strategists were cheered by an IFOP institute poll for the Journal du Dimanche, taken on Friday, suggesting the centre-right had gained three points to stand at 41 percent and the combined left lost 2.5 points at 38.5 percent.

It projected the coalition winning at least a 100-seat National Assembly majority, due to the magnifying effect of the two-round voting system in single-member constituencies, and to a slight decline in the extreme-right National Front vote.

But IFOP political analyst Jean-Luc Parodi cautioned against reading too much into the poll, noting that 27 percent of people certain to vote said they could still change their minds, and that about 100 seats hinged on less than three percentage points in the runoff -- less than the pollsters' margin of error.
Chirac has several opportunities to try to sway the outcome in the next three weeks, starting with a photo opportunity flanked by movie stars at the Cannes festival's 50th anniversary on Sunday.

His diplomatic calendar features a May 15-18 trip to China likely to yield pledges of impressive-sounding contracts for French businesses, a May 20 meeting with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the most popular foreign leader in France, and an informal European Union summit on May 23, all before the first ballot.

He also stands a good chance of hosting a NATO-Russia summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Paris on May 27 -- between the two ballots -- to lay the foundations for post-Cold War European security.
Most commentators also expect the president to make one more direct appeal to the voters for a majority, probably on television, in the final days of the campaign.
Many scored his first bid -- an article in provincial newspapers last week assailing the Socialists' record in power -- as a failure.

But the IFOP poll, though showing that more voters were discontented than satisfied with his intervention, suggested he may have begun to remobilise an apathetic or disenchanted right-wing electorate.

Since he called the early election, Chirac has shifted his ground from seeking a mandate to enter a single European currency from a position of strength to warning against the left's record and platform.

Parodi said his decisive argument in the final days may be to play on fears of a debilitating "cohabitation" between a conservative president and a left-wing government dependent on Eurosceptic Communist votes for a majority.

Most pollsters reckon the right has a key advantage because it has 464 incumbents among the 577 National Assembly members, most of them well rooted in their constituencies and many facing previously unknown opponents.

The left's best hope is to focus on the choice of prime minister between Juppe and Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, and to exploit widespread discontent over record 12.8 percent unemployment and stagnant purchasing power.

The right's strategy is to dodge the Juppe issue by fudging who will be prime minister, and concentrate on attacking the left's "irresponsible" promises to create 700,000 jobs and cut the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.

It is also playing on divisions on European integration between the pro-euro Socialists and the anti-euro Communists, and accusing the left of being soft on illegal immigration, an issue it hopes may win back some voters from the National Front.
